one_line_idea: The synthetic-to-real gap in super-resolution is dominated by unmodeled noise and compression, not by blur-kernel mismatch, so blind-kernel estimation attacks a second-order problem.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Super-resolution models trained on bicubically downsampled pairs degrade sharply on real photographs, and much of the blind-SR literature attributes this gap primarily to unknown blur kernels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Matching realistic sensor noise and compression statistics alone, while keeping a deliberately wrong bicubic kernel, recovers the majority of the synthetic-to-real transfer gap; kernel realism alone recovers only a minority share.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a factorial ablation toggling kernel realism, noise realism, and compression realism independently, the noise and compression factors will show larger main effects on real-photo restoration quality than the kernel factor.
why_important: Blind-kernel estimation is a large subfield; if kernel mismatch is second-order, research effort and model capacity should be redirected toward noise and compression modeling.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual pipelines ablate their own components, but a clean factorial attribution of the synthetic-to-real gap across kernel, noise, and compression with interaction terms may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched SR models on a 2x2x2 factorial of degradation realism (kernel, noise, compression), evaluate all eight on the same held-out real-photo set, and estimate main effects and interactions of each factor on restoration quality.
main_risk: Real degradations entangle the three factors, so a factorial synthetic design may fail to represent real interaction structure and understate the kernel effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Unknown blur kernels are treated as the central obstacle of blind super-resolution, with noise and compression handled as secondary nuisances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Consumer photos are dominated by in-camera denoising and compression whose artifact statistics deviate from training assumptions far more than mild optical blur deviates from bicubic.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one bicubic-only pretrained SR model against one trained with realistic noise plus compression but a bicubic kernel on a handful of real photos; if the second closes most of the visible gap, kernel mismatch is not dominant.

one_line_idea: Large randomized degradation pipelines teach models the artifact statistics of the pipeline itself, and a small set of camera-measured degradations transfers better to real photos.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] State-of-practice real-world SR training uses randomized multi-stage degradation pipelines that compose blur, resize, noise, and compression in shuffled orders with random parameters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on such pipelines overfit to pipeline-specific artifact combinations that rarely occur in real captures, and a compact degradation set measured from a few real camera and ISP configurations yields better real-world transfer at equal training cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A model trained on measured device degradations will outperform a randomized-pipeline model on real photos from held-out devices, despite the randomized pipeline covering a nominally wider degradation space.
why_important: Randomized pipelines are treated as the default recipe for real-world restoration; if measured degradations dominate, data-collection effort should shift from pipeline engineering to degradation measurement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Comparisons between randomized and measured degradations exist implicitly across papers, but a controlled same-architecture same-budget comparison with held-out devices may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture paired or calibrated degradation profiles from a small number of devices, train two matched models (measured set vs randomized pipeline), and evaluate on real photos from devices unseen by both.
main_risk: A small measured set may fail on genuinely out-of-profile degradations, and the result could depend heavily on which devices are sampled.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Wider randomized degradation coverage is assumed to strictly improve real-world robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Coverage in parameter space is not coverage in artifact-statistics space; random composition can generate combinations with measure near zero in reality while undersampling the dense region where real photos live.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute artifact-statistic descriptors of randomized-pipeline outputs and of real degraded photos, and measure distributional overlap; low overlap already undermines the coverage rationale before any model training.

one_line_idea: The composition order of degradations matters more than degradation diversity for real-world restoration transfer.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real image formation applies degradations in a physically fixed order (optics, sensor noise, ISP processing, compression), while synthetic training pipelines often shuffle stage order for augmentation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Holding marginal degradation distributions fixed, training with the physically correct stage order transfers substantially better to real photos than order-shuffled training, because artifact interactions are order-dependent.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Two models trained with identical per-stage parameter distributions but different stage orderings will show a measurable real-photo quality gap in favor of the physical ordering.
why_important: If order dominates, the popular practice of shuffling degradation stages is actively harmful, and pipelines can be improved for free by fixing the order.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Stage shuffling was introduced as a robustness heuristic; an isolated test of ordering with marginals held constant may not have been reported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct two training sets with identical stage parameter distributions, one physically ordered and one shuffled, train matched models, and compare on real degraded photos.
main_risk: The effect may be small relative to noise-model realism, making it hard to detect without large evaluation sets.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shuffled orders are believed to widen coverage and therefore help generalization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Noise applied before blur versus after blur produces categorically different local statistics, so shuffling creates artifact families that never occur in cameras and dilutes training signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Visualize and statistically compare noise-residual distributions of physically ordered versus shuffled pipelines against real photos; if shuffled statistics are far from real ones, order matters before any training run.

one_line_idea: Per-image single-kernel estimation in blind SR is a mis-specified problem because real point-spread functions are spatially varying and chromatically aberrated.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Most blind SR methods estimate one spatially uniform blur kernel per image, while real lens blur varies across the field of view and differs per color channel.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The residual error from forcing a single uniform kernel is larger than the error from moderate kernel misestimation, so improving per-image kernel estimators has hit a floor imposed by the uniformity assumption itself.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Restoration with an oracle spatially varying kernel field will outperform restoration with the best possible single uniform kernel by a margin larger than the spread among competing single-kernel estimators.
why_important: It would explain diminishing returns in kernel-estimation research and redirect effort to spatially varying degradation representations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spatially varying blur is studied in deblurring, but quantifying the uniformity-assumption floor specifically for blind SR pipelines may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate realistic field-varying, channel-dependent blur, then compare restoration quality using the oracle varying kernel field versus the optimal single uniform kernel fit, versus current estimators.
main_risk: For narrow-field crops the spatial variation may be negligible, making the conclusion crop-size dependent.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better single-kernel estimation is assumed to be the path to closing the blind-SR gap.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optical design guarantees corner-versus-center blur differences and lateral chromatic aberration in consumer lenses, so the single-kernel model is physically wrong for full frames.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fit a single kernel to synthetic field-varying blur and measure the reconstruction penalty of the fit alone; if the penalty exceeds typical estimator differences, the assumption is the bottleneck.

one_line_idea: Modeling degradations in the raw sensor domain and passing them through an ISP simulator transfers better than modeling degradations directly in sRGB space.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Camera ISPs apply demosaicing, denoising, sharpening, and tone mapping between the sensor and the sRGB image, yet most SR degradation pipelines synthesize degradations directly in sRGB.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Degradations synthesized in raw and rendered through an ISP model reproduce the correlated, signal-dependent artifact structure of real photos better than sRGB-domain synthesis, yielding stronger real-world restoration transfer.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A model trained on raw-domain-degraded, ISP-rendered pairs will beat an sRGB-degradation model of matched capacity on real consumer photos, especially in low-light and high-ISO conditions.
why_important: It would establish that ISP modeling is a first-class component of restoration training data, changing how the field builds pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Raw-domain denoising is established, but a controlled comparison of raw-plus-ISP degradation synthesis against sRGB synthesis for general SR training may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build two matched training sets, one raw-degraded then ISP-rendered and one sRGB-degraded, train identical models, and compare on real photos across ISO levels.
main_risk: ISP simulators may be inaccurate for modern devices with proprietary neural processing, capping the realism advantage.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] sRGB-space degradation synthesis is assumed adequate as long as parameter ranges are wide.
why_it_might_be_wrong: ISP operations are nonlinear and content-adaptive, so their interaction with sensor noise cannot be replicated by adding independent noise in sRGB.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare noise and edge-artifact statistics of sRGB-synthesized degradations against real high-ISO photos and against raw-plus-ISP synthesis; a persistent statistics gap for sRGB synthesis is immediate evidence.

one_line_idea: Replacing additive white Gaussian noise with signal-dependent heteroscedastic noise is the single largest lever in degradation modeling for real-world SR.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Sensor noise is signal-dependent (approximately Poisson-Gaussian in raw), yet additive white Gaussian noise remains a common component of SR degradation pipelines.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Among all single-component realism upgrades to a bicubic baseline pipeline, upgrading the noise model to a calibrated signal-dependent form produces the largest real-photo transfer improvement.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a leave-one-in study where exactly one pipeline component is made realistic at a time, the noise-model upgrade will rank first on real low-light photos and remain top-two on general real photo sets.
why_important: It gives practitioners a priority order for pipeline improvements instead of the current everything-at-once pipeline engineering.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Component-wise realism upgrades are common, but a ranked single-component attribution across noise, kernel, compression, and resampling may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models each with exactly one realistic component added to a bicubic baseline, and rank their real-photo improvements.
main_risk: The ranking may be content-dependent (low light versus daylight), preventing a single universal ordering.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners treat noise realism, kernel realism, and compression realism as roughly interchangeable contributors to robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Signal dependence changes where noise appears (shadows versus highlights), which is exactly the structure denoising-entangled SR must learn; white noise teaches the wrong spatial prior.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate an AWGN-trained model on synthetic heteroscedastic noise and vice versa; a large asymmetry in cross-noise degradation already indicates the noise model is a first-order factor.

one_line_idea: Degradation pipelines undersample the mild-degradation regime that dominates real photos, so blind models are miscalibrated toward over-restoration of nearly clean inputs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic degradation pipelines sample parameter ranges chosen to be challenging, while a large fraction of real user photos are only mildly degraded.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The mismatch between the training severity distribution and the deployment severity distribution causes systematic over-sharpening and hallucination on mildly degraded inputs, and reweighting training severity toward the deployment distribution fixes it without hurting hard cases much.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A severity-reweighted model will show fewer artifacts on near-clean inputs and comparable performance on heavily degraded inputs, compared to a standard pipeline model of equal capacity.
why_important: Deployment-weighted training data design is cheap and could remove a common, user-visible failure class of restoration products.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Severity distributions are usually reported as ranges, not matched to deployment statistics; explicit severity-distribution matching may be unstudied for SR.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate a severity distribution from a real photo corpus using no-reference degradation estimators, retrain with importance-weighted severity sampling, and compare artifact rates on mild inputs.
main_risk: No-reference severity estimation is noisy, so the deployment distribution estimate may be biased.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Training on hard degradations is assumed to make easy cases trivially safe.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A model optimized under a heavy-degradation prior rationally infers heavy degradation everywhere and thus over-corrects clean content; easy cases are not automatically safe under distribution mismatch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Feed visibly clean, high-quality photos to popular blind restoration models and count over-sharpening and texture-invention artifacts; a high artifact rate on clean input demonstrates the miscalibration directly.

one_line_idea: Modern phone photos are already processed by on-device neural enhancement, so the dominant real-world degradation family is neural-network-induced, and classic degradation models are increasingly obsolete.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Current smartphones apply learned processing (multi-frame fusion, learned denoising, super-resolution-like sharpening) before a user ever sees the image.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The residual degradations in modern phone photos are dominated by artifacts of on-device neural processing (over-smoothing, texture invention, fusion ghosting) that classic blur-noise-compression pipelines do not model, causing restoration models to misfire on the newest devices.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Restoration models trained on classic pipelines will show a larger quality gap on recent-device photos than on decade-old-device photos, controlling for scene content.
why_important: The field may be optimizing for a degradation distribution that is disappearing from the real world.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Neural-ISP artifacts are discussed anecdotally, but treating neural processing artifacts as a first-class degradation family with its own synthesis models may be new for SR training.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect photos of matched scenes from older and newer devices, run classic-pipeline restoration models on both, and compare failure rates and artifact types.
main_risk: Device processing is proprietary and version-dependent, making the degradation family a moving target that is hard to model canonically.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Blur, noise, downsampling, and compression are assumed to remain a sufficient basis for real-world degradation modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned enhancement replaces stochastic noise with structured, content-correlated errors; a pipeline built from independent stochastic stages cannot express such errors at all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inspect residuals between recent-phone outputs and tripod raw captures of the same scene; if residuals are structured and content-correlated rather than noise-like, classic pipelines are missing the dominant family.

one_line_idea: Many practically low-quality images were never downsampled, so framing super-resolution as inverse downsampling is a category error for a large share of use cases.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SR is formalized as inverting a downsampling operator, yet many low-detail real images are natively low-detail due to defocus, motion, atmospheric effects, or simply distant subjects at native resolution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For natively low-detail images, models trained as downsampling inverters produce characteristic failure modes (wrong detail scale, gridded texture) that a detail-synthesis formulation without a downsampling assumption avoids.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a corpus of natively low-detail photos that were never resampled, an SR model will underperform a matched restoration model trained on optical-degradation-only pairs at identical resolution.
why_important: It questions whether the field's core operator assumption matches deployment, and suggests splitting SR into resampling inversion and detail restoration as distinct tasks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The distinction between resampled and natively soft images is rarely made operational in benchmark construction or model design.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble two matched evaluation sets, one genuinely downsampled and one natively soft at identical apparent detail level, and compare failure patterns of standard SR models across the two.
main_risk: Constructing natively soft images with known ground truth is hard; proxy ground truths may bias the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats scale-factor SR as the canonical formulation covering practical low-quality imagery.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The forward operators differ fundamentally: resampling aliases high frequencies while optics attenuate them smoothly, so the correct inverse priors differ too.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a standard 4x SR model on soft-but-full-resolution photos (upsampling not needed) via downsample-then-restore, and compare against a deblurring model; systematic SR-specific artifacts would appear immediately.

one_line_idea: Blind-SR kernel estimates are echoes of the learned image prior rather than measurements, and they collapse on images that violate natural-image statistics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] From a single low-resolution image, the blur kernel and the high-resolution content are not jointly identifiable without a prior; blind-SR estimators resolve this with learned natural-image priors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Kernel estimators primarily report the kernel that reconciles the input with the natural-image prior, so on non-natural content (synthetic patterns, text, star fields) their estimates become systematically wrong in predictable directions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying standard kernel estimators to images with known kernels but non-natural statistics will produce errors far larger than on natural images with the same kernels, with error direction correlated to the prior mismatch.
why_important: It reframes kernel estimation as prior-dependent inference, cautioning against using estimated kernels as physical measurements in scientific or forensic settings.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Identifiability is acknowledged theoretically, but a systematic study of prior-induced kernel bias on out-of-prior content may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Blur natural and non-natural image sets with identical known kernels, run public kernel estimators on both, and compare error magnitude and structure.
main_risk: Estimator failures on non-natural content might be dismissed as out-of-scope rather than as evidence about the mechanism.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Kernel estimation is implicitly treated as approximate measurement of a physical quantity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Without identifiability, any single-image estimator must lean on the prior; the estimate is a function of both image and prior, which becomes obvious exactly where the prior is wrong.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Blur a sharp text screenshot and a natural photo with the same known kernel and compare estimated kernels from one public method; a large discrepancy demonstrates prior dependence within minutes.

one_line_idea: A few minutes of per-device calibration beats universal blind restoration, because devices cluster tightly in degradation space.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Blind restoration aims to handle arbitrary unknown degradations, while any physical device has a stable, measurable degradation profile.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Conditioning a restoration model on a lightweight per-device degradation fingerprint, obtained from a few calibration captures, outperforms state-of-the-art blind restoration on that device by a margin that no realistic amount of blind training data closes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Fingerprint-conditioned restoration will beat blind restoration on held-out photos from calibrated devices, and the gain will persist even when the blind model is trained with substantially more data.
why_important: It suggests the field over-invests in the fully blind setting when a practical calibrate-once workflow could dominate for the common case of a known device.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Device-conditioned restoration exists in raw denoising, but a general SR-and-restoration framework built around cheap consumer-side calibration may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a calibration protocol (a few chart or scene captures), learn fingerprint embeddings, train a fingerprint-conditioned model, and compare against blind baselines on held-out photos from the same devices.
main_risk: Degradation profiles drift with firmware updates, scene modes, and shooting conditions, potentially invalidating stale fingerprints.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The blind setting is treated as the practically relevant one because users will not calibrate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Calibration can be invisible to users (metadata plus a handful of everyday shots), and per-device consistency is exactly the structure blind models are forced to marginalize over.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For two devices, fine-tune a small adapter per device on a handful of self-captured pairs and compare with the blind baseline; a clear win on both devices is quick directional evidence.

one_line_idea: A degradation-space distance between training pipeline outputs and real photos predicts real-world transfer better than benchmark scores do.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners select restoration training pipelines by validating on synthetic benchmarks, and synthetic scores often fail to predict real-world quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A distributional distance computed in a space of artifact statistics (noise spectra, edge profiles, block-artifact features) between pipeline-degraded images and a target real corpus predicts a model's real-world performance better than its synthetic benchmark score.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across many pipeline variants, the artifact-space distance will correlate more strongly with human-rated real-photo restoration quality than synthetic PSNR or perceptual scores do.
why_important: It would give the field a cheap, model-free tool for designing degradation pipelines before any training run.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distribution matching is used implicitly, but a validated predictive metric for pipeline-to-deployment transfer may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a grid of models over pipeline variants, obtain human ratings on a fixed real-photo set, and compare rank correlations of the artifact-space distance versus synthetic scores with human ratings.
main_risk: The metric depends on choosing artifact features well; a poor feature space would fail without disproving the general idea.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic validation scores are treated as the primary signal for pipeline design.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synthetic scores measure fit to the pipeline itself, which is circular; distance-to-deployment measures the thing that actually varies at test time.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For a handful of existing public models with known training pipelines, compute artifact-space distances to one real corpus and check whether the ordering matches informal community judgments of real-world quality.

one_line_idea: Real-world paired SR benchmarks reward slight blur because zoom-lens pair alignment errors make hedged, soft predictions optimal under full-reference metrics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real-world SR datasets built by capturing the same scene at different focal lengths require subpixel registration, which is imperfect, and full-reference metrics penalize spatial misalignment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The residual misalignment in paired real-world benchmarks makes slightly blurred predictions score better than sharp, correctly restored ones, so leaderboard optimization on these datasets systematically selects for blur.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Adding a small learned blur to a sharp model's output will improve its full-reference score on misaligned real-world pairs while decreasing human-rated sharpness, and the score gain will vanish on synthetically aligned data.
why_important: If true, the datasets meant to fix synthetic-training bias introduce an opposite bias, and conclusions drawn from them about method superiority are suspect.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Misalignment-tolerant losses exist, but quantifying how much benchmark rankings are driven by alignment hedging may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate per-pair misalignment on a real-world benchmark, stratify evaluation by alignment quality, and test whether method rankings change between well-aligned and poorly aligned strata.
main_risk: Alignment estimation itself is imperfect and could confound the stratification.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Real-world paired benchmarks are treated as strictly more trustworthy than synthetic ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A metric that penalizes any spatial offset turns registration error into a blur reward; the physics of the capture process guarantees some registration error.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Apply small Gaussian blurs of increasing width to one strong model's outputs on a real-world paired set and plot the full-reference score; a non-monotone curve peaking at nonzero blur confirms the hedging incentive.

one_line_idea: Unpaired real-world restoration methods secretly depend on the same hand-crafted degradation assumptions they claim to avoid.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Unpaired approaches learn degradations from real low-quality images without paired supervision, marketed as assumption-free alternatives to synthetic pipelines.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The degradation generators inside unpaired methods are constrained (architecture, losses, cycle constraints) in ways that encode nearly the same blur-noise-compression family as hand-crafted pipelines, so they fail on degradation types outside that family just like synthetic training does.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On degradation families absent from the implicit inductive bias (for example fusion ghosting or scanning artifacts), unpaired methods will fail at rates comparable to synthetic-pipeline baselines despite training on real data containing those artifacts.
why_important: It challenges the claimed generality of unpaired learning and clarifies that the bottleneck is degradation representation, not pairing.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Critiques of unpaired restoration exist, but an audit of what degradation families the learned generators can and cannot express may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train an unpaired method on a corpus containing exotic artifacts, inspect whether its learned degradation generator reproduces them, and measure restoration quality on those artifacts versus in-family ones.
main_risk: Failures could be attributed to optimization difficulties rather than representational limits, requiring careful controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Learning degradations from data is assumed to capture whatever is present in the real corpus.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A generator can only express what its architecture and objectives allow; cycle-consistency and adversarial losses are known to under-constrain and simplify the learned forward model.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Sample from a trained unpaired degradation generator and compare artifact statistics against the real corpus; missing artifact families in the samples reveal the representational ceiling without any restoration evaluation.

one_line_idea: Per-image test-time adaptation from internal recurrence beats adding more pretraining data for real-world restoration at foundation scale.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Single-image internal statistics (cross-scale patch recurrence) suffice to train small image-specific SR models, an approach eclipsed by large externally trained models.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For real photos with atypical degradations, briefly adapting a large pretrained restoration model to the test image's internal statistics yields larger quality gains than scaling the pretraining set by an order of magnitude.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A mid-sized model plus per-image adaptation will match or beat a much larger or longer-trained static model on out-of-pipeline real photos, while losing slightly on in-pipeline synthetic benchmarks.
why_important: It would reorder the field's investment from ever-larger pretraining toward adaptive inference, with major deployment implications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Internal-statistics adaptation predates large restoration models; a rigorous adaptation-versus-scale tradeoff study in the current regime may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take checkpoints of one architecture trained with increasing data budgets, add a fixed per-image adaptation procedure to each, and map quality gains from adaptation versus gains from data scale on real out-of-distribution photos.
main_risk: Per-image adaptation cost may be prohibitive for consumer latency budgets, limiting practical relevance even if quality wins.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scaling data and parameters is assumed to dominate any test-time trick.
why_it_might_be_wrong: No fixed training distribution can cover device-specific and image-specific degradation quirks; the test image is the only unimpeachable sample of its own degradation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On a handful of atypically degraded photos, run a public restoration model with and without a short self-supervised fine-tune on the test image itself and compare visible quality.

one_line_idea: Blind restoration models violate a do-no-harm principle on clean inputs, and identity preservation on high-quality images should be a mandatory reported metric.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration models are deployed in pipelines where input quality is unknown and sometimes already high, yet evaluation almost exclusively uses degraded inputs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Current blind restoration models measurably corrupt already-clean inputs (over-sharpening, texture replacement, tone shifts), and a simple identity-preservation metric on clean inputs would reveal large differences between models that current benchmarks hide.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Popular blind restoration models will show substantial deviation from identity on clean high-quality inputs, and the deviation ranking will differ from the degraded-input quality ranking.
why_important: In real products, harming good inputs is often worse than under-restoring bad ones; the field has no standard measurement of this risk.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Clean-input behavior is occasionally shown qualitatively, but a standardized do-no-harm benchmark with quantitative identity metrics may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a verified-clean image set, run blind restoration models on it, and report deviation-from-input metrics alongside standard degraded-input benchmarks.
main_risk: Defining verified-clean is nontrivial since all images have some degradation; threshold choices could be contested.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Models good at restoring degraded images are assumed approximately harmless on clean ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Blind models must infer degradation severity, and severity estimation has irreducible error; under a training prior of heavy degradation, clean inputs are out-of-distribution and provoke confident over-correction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run several public restoration models on a few pristine photographs and measure pixel and perceptual deviation from input; visible texture replacement on any pristine image makes the point immediately.

one_line_idea: Blind restoration fails as a cliff, not a slope, just outside its training severity range, and the cliff location is predictable from training data alone.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Blind restoration models are trained on bounded degradation parameter ranges, while deployment severity is unbounded.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model quality degrades gracefully within the training severity envelope but collapses abruptly just beyond it, and the collapse point can be predicted from the training distribution without running the model on extreme inputs.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping degradation severity continuously will reveal a sharp quality knee near the training range boundary across architectures, with knee location tracking the training range rather than model capacity.
why_important: A predictable failure boundary enables severity-gating in products (refuse or route inputs beyond the knee) instead of silent catastrophic outputs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Out-of-range behavior is anecdotally known, but a systematic severity-sweep characterization with knee-prediction from training statistics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train models with deliberately different severity ranges, sweep test severity finely, locate quality knees, and test whether knees align with training boundaries.
main_risk: Some architectures may extrapolate better than others, blurring the knee and weakening the universal-cliff claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Degradation robustness is assumed to fade gradually as inputs get harder.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration is inverse inference under a learned degradation prior; outside the prior's support, the posterior is dominated by the image prior alone, which produces a qualitative regime change rather than gradual decay.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public blind model with a documented training range, sweep noise strength through and past the range on a few images, and plot quality; a visible knee at the boundary is quick confirmation.

one_line_idea: A small mixture-of-experts routed by degradation archetype beats a monolithic blind model of equal total capacity on real photos.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real degraded photos cluster around a few archetypes (out-of-focus, motion blur, low-light noise, heavy compression, old-photo damage), while blind models handle all cases with shared weights.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Marginalizing over degradation archetypes in one network forces averaged inverse operators; explicit routing to archetype experts removes this averaging penalty and wins at matched total parameters and training compute.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The routed mixture will beat the monolithic model most on inputs far from archetype boundaries and lose only on genuinely mixed degradations, netting a clear overall gain on real photo sets.
why_important: It challenges the assumption that generalist restoration models are the right scaling recipe and offers an interpretable, debuggable alternative.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Degradation-aware conditioning exists, but a controlled equal-capacity mixture-versus-monolith comparison on real archetype-labeled photos may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Label a real photo corpus by degradation archetype, train a router plus experts and a matched monolith on identical data, and compare per-archetype and overall quality.
main_risk: Router errors on ambiguous inputs could cause worst-case failures exceeding the monolith's averaged behavior.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A single sufficiently large blind model is expected to internalize routing implicitly and dominate explicit mixtures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Different archetypes require nearly opposite inverse operators (for example sharpening versus denoising priorities), and shared weights must compromise unless capacity is wasted on redundancy.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare a monolithic blind model against per-archetype fine-tuned copies of the same checkpoint, each evaluated only on its archetype; a large specialist advantage bounds the routing upside from above.

one_line_idea: A single user-facing fidelity-versus-enhancement dial captures most practical value of degradation estimation, making precise automatic estimation unnecessary for consumer restoration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Substantial research effort goes into estimating degradation parameters automatically so restoration strength can be set correctly.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Human users given one scalar control over restoration aggressiveness reach output quality within a small margin of oracle degradation-aware restoration, so the practical value of automatic degradation estimation is far lower than its research prominence suggests.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a user study, self-tuned single-dial restoration will be preferred nearly as often as oracle-parameter restoration and substantially more often than fixed-strength blind restoration.
why_important: It reframes part of blind restoration as an interaction-design problem rather than an estimation problem, redirecting research priorities.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Controllable restoration exists, but quantifying how much of the estimation problem a single human-set scalar absorbs may not have been measured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a strength-conditioned restoration model, run a user study comparing fixed-strength, user-dialed, and oracle-parameter modes, and measure preference and adjustment time.
main_risk: One scalar may be insufficient when multiple degradation axes need independent correction, limiting the claim to common cases.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Accurate automatic degradation estimation is treated as necessary for high-quality blind restoration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration quality is ultimately judged by the user, and a preference judgment collapses many degradation parameters into one perceived-aggressiveness axis that a dial exposes directly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Give a few users a strength slider on a small controllable model and record whether their chosen outputs approach oracle-strength outputs on images with known degradations.

one_line_idea: The blind restoration setting ignores freely available capture metadata that carries most of the degradation information the models struggle to estimate.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Most real photos carry metadata (device model, ISO, exposure time, aperture, compression settings) that constrains the degradation, yet blind restoration research defines the problem as image-only.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Conditioning restoration on standard capture metadata recovers a large fraction of the gap between blind and oracle-degradation restoration, at zero estimation cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A metadata-conditioned model will significantly beat an image-only blind model on real photos with intact metadata, with the largest gains on high-ISO and long-exposure images.
why_important: If metadata closes much of the gap, the purely blind setting is an artificial hardening of the problem that mismatches deployment reality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Metadata is used in raw processing research, but systematic metadata conditioning for general blind SR and restoration may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without metadata conditioning on a real paired or pseudo-paired corpus and compare on held-out devices, stratified by ISO.
main_risk: Metadata is stripped by many platforms, so gains may not transfer to redistributed images, though first-party applications retain it.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The image-only blind setting is treated as the practically motivated formulation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Device plus ISO nearly determines the noise model, and noise is a dominant degradation factor, so ignoring metadata discards the strongest available conditioning signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Bin a real photo set by ISO from metadata, apply noise-level-conditioned restoration using the bin as the level, and compare against blind estimation of noise level on the same images.

one_line_idea: Restoration models fail systematically on non-photographic content because both degradation models and image priors are photo-centric, and a content-type failure taxonomy would expose this blind spot.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration models are trained almost exclusively on photographs, while real usage includes scanned documents, screenshots, illustrations, maps, and rendered graphics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On non-photographic content, restoration models exhibit reproducible failure families (halo artifacts on flat-color edges, texture invention on smooth fills, font distortion) whose severity is predictable from the content type, and light content-type conditioning removes most of these failures.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A content-type-stratified evaluation will show failure rates on non-photographic classes that are multiples of photographic failure rates for the same models, and per-type adapters will close most of the gap.
why_important: Non-photographic images are ubiquitous in practice (documents, UI captures), and their silent corruption by photo-centric restorers is a real product hazard.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Document-specific enhancement exists, but a unified failure taxonomy of general restoration models across content types may not have been built.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct degraded versions of documents, screenshots, and illustrations with known ground truth, evaluate general restoration models, and catalog failure families per content type.
main_risk: The taxonomy could fragment into endless subtypes, making the result descriptive rather than actionable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] General restoration models are assumed to degrade gracefully on non-photographic inputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both halves of the inverse problem (degradation model and prior) encode photographic statistics; on synthetic-flat content the prior injects photographic texture where none belongs, which is corruption rather than graceful degradation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Downsample and compress a text screenshot and an illustration, restore with a popular blind model, and inspect for invented texture and font damage; failures are typically visible on the first examples.

one_line_idea: Analog degradations in old photos form a structurally different family from digital ones, and models trained on digital pipelines hallucinate when facing film-era artifacts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Old-photo restoration confronts physical degradations (scratches, chemical fading, film grain, halftone printing, paper texture) that differ mechanistically from digital blur-noise-compression.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Digital-pipeline-trained models misinterpret analog artifacts as content or as digital noise, producing characteristic hallucinations, and explicit analog degradation synthesis (grain models, scratch simulation, halftone patterns) fixes most failures without any architecture change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Adding physically motivated analog degradation synthesis to training will reduce hallucination and artifact-misinterpretation rates on real archival photos compared to matched digital-only training.
why_important: Archival restoration is a socially valuable application where hallucination (invented faces, altered documents) is especially harmful.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Old-photo restoration is studied, but a controlled attribution showing that degradation synthesis rather than architecture drives archival quality may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build an analog degradation simulator, train matched models with and without it, and evaluate on genuinely old photographs using human artifact annotation.
main_risk: No ground truth exists for real archival photos, forcing reliance on human judgment or simulated proxies.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Wide digital degradation pipelines are assumed to subsume analog artifacts as edge cases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Analog artifacts are structured, spatially correlated, and multiplicative in ways digital pipelines never synthesize; a model cannot invert an operator family it has never seen.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a strong digital-pipeline model on a few scanned film photos with visible grain and scratches and inspect whether grain becomes texture and scratches become objects; such misreadings are quick to spot.

one_line_idea: The practically relevant perception-distortion tradeoff is per-region, not per-model, and a single global operating point is wrong for most images.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The perception-distortion tradeoff is analyzed and reported as a property of models, each occupying one point on the tradeoff curve, while images contain regions with very different stakes (faces, text, textures, flat sky).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Human preference is maximized by spatially varying the tradeoff (high fidelity on faces and text, high perceptual quality on stochastic textures), and a spatially adaptive model beats every fixed-tradeoff model on overall preference.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A model with region-adaptive tradeoff control will win human preference against fixed-tradeoff baselines spanning the curve, and the win margin will grow with image semantic complexity.
why_important: It changes the design target from choosing a tradeoff point to learning a tradeoff policy over image content.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Region-aware losses exist, but formulating and validating a spatial tradeoff policy against the standard per-model tradeoff framing may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a restoration model conditioned on a spatial tradeoff map, derive maps from semantic segmentation, and run preference studies against fixed-point baselines.
main_risk: Spatially varying treatment risks visible inconsistency at region boundaries, which could dominate preference negatively.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The tradeoff is treated as a scalar model property to be chosen once per method.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The cost of hallucination is semantic and varies by orders of magnitude across regions; no single scalar operating point can be optimal under a spatially varying cost.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Composite outputs of an existing fidelity-oriented model on face and text regions with a perceptual model elsewhere, and check in a small preference test whether the composite beats both sources.

one_line_idea: Learned perceptual metrics are gameable by artifact styles matched to their training distribution, and metric-tuned SR models exhibit a recognizable metric texture.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Learned full-reference perceptual similarity metrics and learned no-reference quality metrics are trained on finite distortion distributions and are widely used as SR training losses and evaluation criteria.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Optimizing restoration outputs against learned metrics produces a systematic, classifiable texture signature that scores well under the metric while diverging from natural image statistics, and human raters can learn to spot it.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A classifier will distinguish metric-optimized outputs from naturally sharp images at high accuracy using texture statistics alone, and metric scores will overestimate human preference specifically on metric-optimized outputs.
why_important: If metric texture exists, cross-paper comparisons using these metrics measure metric exploitation rather than perceptual quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Metric gaming is suspected informally, but a demonstration that metric-optimized restoration has a detectable universal signature may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train restoration models with increasing weight on a learned metric, collect outputs, train a signature classifier, and correlate metric-versus-human disagreement with signature strength.
main_risk: The signature may be model-family specific rather than universal, weakening the general claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Learned perceptual metrics are treated as robust drop-in proxies for human judgment in both training and evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Any differentiable metric defines a direction of maximal score increase; optimization pressure concentrates outputs along that direction, which is a distribution the metric's training data never covered.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Directly optimize a few images to improve a learned metric score under a fidelity constraint and inspect the emerging texture; visible non-natural texture with improved scores demonstrates the exploit quickly.

one_line_idea: Human preference between faithful and hallucinated restorations reverses with viewing time and ground-truth knowledge, so time-limited studies structurally favor hallucination.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration papers rely on quick pairwise preference judgments, typically with short viewing times and no access to reference content.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Preference for sharp hallucinated outputs at short exposures flips toward fidelity-preserving outputs under extended inspection, zoom access, or when raters know the true content, meaning current protocols encode a hallucination bias into the field's optimization target.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The preference share of a generative restorer over a fidelity restorer will drop measurably as viewing time increases and again when references or content familiarity are introduced.
why_important: The field tunes models against human studies; if the protocol biases the verdict, the whole perceptual-SR direction is optimizing a lab artifact.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Viewing-time effects are known in psychophysics broadly, but their specific impact on restoration preference protocols may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the same pairwise comparisons across controlled exposure durations, with and without reference images, and measure preference reversal rates.
main_risk: Longer inspection may increase noise or attention artifacts rather than genuine preference change, requiring careful protocol design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Quick preference judgments are assumed to reflect stable perceptual quality rankings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hallucination is detectable only through scrutiny or knowledge; a protocol that denies raters both is blind to the exact failure that distinguishes the compared methods.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Rerun a small subset of an existing comparison at two exposure times (brief versus unlimited with zoom) and check for preference shifts on hallucination-prone content like faces and text.

one_line_idea: The empirical perception-distortion frontier is largely a loss mis-specification artifact, and a properly specified conditional likelihood model can dominate both endpoints simultaneously.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The perception-distortion tradeoff theorem bounds joint performance, but the empirical frontier occupied by current models is not known to be near the theoretical bound.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Much of the practically observed tradeoff arises from mis-specified losses (pixel regression versus adversarial mixtures) rather than from the information-theoretic limit, so models trained with better-specified posterior objectives can improve perception and distortion together relative to today's frontier.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A restoration model trained with a principled posterior-matching objective will land strictly inside the current empirical frontier, improving both metric families at once at matched capacity.
why_important: It determines whether the field should treat the tradeoff as a budget to allocate or as slack to eliminate.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The theorem is often cited as if current models sit on the bound; an explicit slack-measurement research program may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix architecture and data, train with several objective families including posterior-matching ones, plot the empirical frontier, and measure movement of the frontier itself rather than movement along it.
main_risk: Posterior-matching objectives are hard to optimize at scale and failures could be blamed on optimization rather than the hypothesis.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Improving perceptual quality is assumed to require sacrificing distortion roughly along the observed curve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The theoretical bound constrains distributions, not training losses; there is no evidence that adversarially trained regressors achieve the bound, leaving room to dominate both axes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one small inverse problem with tractable posterior (synthetic degradation on a toy image family), compare the empirical tradeoff of standard losses against the analytic posterior; measured slack demonstrates the artifact.

one_line_idea: On real-world paired datasets, the reported perception-distortion tradeoff is confounded by ground-truth misalignment, which taxes fidelity-oriented models more than generative ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real-world SR datasets contain registration errors between low-resolution and high-resolution pairs, and distortion metrics are alignment-sensitive while perceptual metrics are more tolerant.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Misalignment inflates measured distortion for faithful models without similarly penalizing generative models, so part of the published tradeoff on real-world data is a measurement artifact of alignment error interacting with metric sensitivity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] After alignment-aware evaluation (local registration before metric computation), the measured gap between fidelity-oriented and perception-oriented models on real-world pairs will shrink substantially compared to naive evaluation.
why_important: Conclusions about how much fidelity must be sacrificed for realism on real data drive method choices; a confounded measurement misleads the field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Alignment-robust metrics exist, but re-auditing published tradeoff claims on real-world datasets under alignment correction may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a spectrum of models on a real-world paired set with naive metrics and with alignment-corrected metrics, and compare the resulting tradeoff curves.
main_risk: Alignment correction can itself remove genuine model errors, over-correcting and biasing the comparison the other way.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Tradeoff measurements on real-world paired data are treated as more authoritative than synthetic ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A fidelity model reproducing the true scene geometry is penalized for the dataset's registration error, while a generative model synthesizing plausible texture is not; this asymmetry mimics a tradeoff.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one faithful model's outputs, apply small local registration to the ground truth before computing distortion, and observe how much of the reported fidelity deficit disappears.

one_line_idea: Replacing distortion-to-reference with consistency-to-observation as the fidelity axis makes the perception tradeoff much milder, and consistency should be the reported fidelity metric for generative restoration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fidelity in SR is measured as distortion against one reference image, although for generative restorers the operationally meaningful constraint is agreement with the degraded observation under the forward model.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Perceptual quality conflicts strongly with single-reference distortion but only weakly with observation consistency, so reframing fidelity as data consistency reveals that high realism and high fidelity-to-evidence are jointly achievable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across models, the correlation between perceptual quality and observation-consistency error will be much weaker than the correlation between perceptual quality and reference distortion, and some generative models will be near-perfectly consistent while scoring poorly on distortion.
why_important: It would legitimize generative restoration where it is evidence-consistent and expose it where it is not, replacing a misleading fidelity axis.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-consistency constraints are standard in inverse-problem solvers, but recasting the perception-distortion debate around measured consistency may be unexplored as an evaluation program.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a set of restoration models with known or estimated forward operators, compute observation-consistency residuals and perceptual scores, and map the empirical tradeoff in the new axes.
main_risk: The forward operator is unknown for blind settings, making consistency measurement itself an estimation problem.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Distortion to the reference is treated as the definition of fidelity in restoration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The reference is one posterior sample, not the evidence; penalizing distance to it punishes legitimate posterior diversity while missing genuine evidence violations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-degrade outputs of several public models with the known synthetic forward operator and compare residual-to-observation against their reference distortion; discordance between the two fidelity notions is immediate evidence.

one_line_idea: Human-preferred restorations systematically degrade machine consumption (OCR, recognition), so perceptual quality and machine quality are diverging objectives needing separate outputs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restored images are consumed both by humans and by downstream machine systems, while restoration models are tuned to human preference or its proxies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Perceptually tuned restoration alters or destroys machine-relevant evidence (glyph shapes, fine boundaries, texture statistics) such that recognition systems perform worse on human-preferred restorations than on distortion-optimized ones of the same inputs.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across matched models, machine task accuracy on restored images will rank inversely with human preference on hallucination-prone content, with the gap concentrated in text and fine-structure regions.
why_important: Pipelines increasingly insert restoration before analysis; if perceptual tuning harms analysis, deployment guidance must change.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Task-driven restoration exists, but a systematic divergence study between human preference and machine accuracy across restoration operating points may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Restore a document-and-scene corpus with fidelity-oriented and perception-oriented models, run standard OCR and recognition systems, and correlate task accuracy with human preference scores.
main_risk: Divergence may vary strongly by task, complicating a clean general conclusion.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better-looking restorations are assumed to be better inputs for downstream systems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human preference rewards plausible texture, but recognition depends on evidence preservation; texture synthesis and evidence preservation are different objectives that coincide only by accident.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run OCR on perceptually restored versus fidelity-restored low-quality text photos and compare character error rates; a consistent gap on a handful of images settles the direction quickly.

one_line_idea: Restoration models should output a hallucination map, and cross-seed variance of generative restorers already provides one that flags fabricated regions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative restoration outputs mix recovered evidence and prior-invented content with no indication of which is which.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-pixel dispersion across sampling seeds is a usable hallucination indicator: regions with high cross-seed variance are dominated by prior invention, and exposing this map materially changes user trust decisions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Cross-seed variance maps will overlap substantially with regions where outputs deviate from ground truth on synthetic tasks, and will flag most human-identified hallucinations on real tasks.
why_important: A standard hallucination-disclosure output would make generative restoration auditable, which matters for forensic, journalistic, and archival uses.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Sample diversity is studied as a quality, but standardizing seed-variance as a hallucination disclosure channel with validation against ground truth may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate multiple seeds per input on synthetic pairs, compute variance maps, and measure overlap with actual error maps; then validate on real images with human hallucination annotation.
main_risk: Consistently wrong regions (confident hallucination across seeds) evade the variance signal, so the map has a known blind spot.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration outputs are presented as single images, with uncertainty communication considered out of scope.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where evidence constrains the posterior, seeds agree; where the prior dominates, seeds disagree; this is exactly the recoverable-versus-invented distinction users need, available at zero training cost.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Sample a public diffusion restorer several times on one degraded face or text image, compute the pixel variance map, and check visually whether high-variance regions coincide with implausible or fabricated detail.

one_line_idea: Perceived restoration quality saturates under realistic viewing conditions, and beyond a resolvable-detail threshold the field is optimizing differences invisible to users.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration evaluation uses magnified crops and pixel-level metrics, while deployed images are viewed at finite display sizes, resolutions, and distances.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under representative viewing conditions, preference differences between recent top restoration models vanish for a large fraction of images, meaning reported improvements increasingly live below the visibility threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Preference studies at realistic viewing scales will show no significant difference between models that differ clearly under magnified inspection, with the null result concentrating in mild-degradation images.
why_important: It calibrates how much of leaderboard progress delivers user-perceivable value and argues for viewing-condition-aware evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Psychophysics of display viewing is mature, but injecting viewing-condition realism into SR evaluation protocols may be rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rerun pairwise comparisons of recent models under controlled realistic viewing (fixed display size and distance, no zoom) and measure how many previously significant gaps survive.
main_risk: Choosing representative viewing conditions is contestable, and results will vary across usage scenarios like print versus mobile.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Metric and crop-level improvements are assumed to translate into user-visible improvements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The human contrast sensitivity function imposes hard limits at typical angular resolutions; differences confined to frequencies beyond that limit cannot be seen regardless of their metric magnitude.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Display outputs of two recent models side by side at typical phone scale to a few viewers without zoom and count discrimination accuracy; chance-level discrimination on many images is quick evidence.

one_line_idea: GAN-versus-diffusion differences in restoration quality are dominated by training data and loss weighting rather than the generative framework itself.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The field has largely migrated from adversarial to diffusion-based restoration, attributing quality gains to the framework change, but migrations also changed data scale, backbones, and losses simultaneously.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under matched backbone, data, and compute, adversarial and diffusion restoration reach statistically comparable perceptual quality, and the perceived diffusion advantage mostly reflects confounded comparisons.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A controlled same-data same-backbone comparison will show framework differences smaller than differences induced by data curation choices within either framework.
why_important: Framework choice drives large engineering investments and inference-cost decisions; if the framework is second-order, cheaper adversarial inference may be preferable for products.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Controlled framework comparisons exist for generation, but a rigorous confound-free comparison specifically for restoration may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train adversarial and diffusion restoration heads on the identical frozen backbone, data, and augmentation, match compute, and run human preference studies plus artifact audits.
main_risk: Matching compute fairly across frameworks is nontrivial since diffusion spends compute at inference.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Diffusion is assumed intrinsically superior for perceptual restoration quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both frameworks can represent the same conditional distributions in principle; observed gaps have plausible mundane explanations in data and tuning asymmetries accumulated across publication waves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public adversarial restorer and one public diffusion restorer of similar vintage and data, and run a small blind preference study; a near-tie would already question the framework narrative.

one_line_idea: Hallucination severity in generative SR scales with prior strength: the better the generative model, the more confidently it fabricates the wrong content.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative restoration combines observation evidence with a learned image prior, and stronger priors produce more plausible-looking detail.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] As the prior improves (more data, larger models), fabricated content becomes simultaneously more plausible and less faithful in evidence-poor regions, so semantic hallucination rate on ambiguous inputs increases with prior quality rather than decreasing.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a scale ladder of generative restorers, human-verified semantic error rate on ambiguous inputs (unreadable text, small faces) will stay flat or rise with scale, while plausibility ratings of the same wrong content rise.
why_important: It contradicts the assumption that scaling fixes hallucination and implies restoration needs explicit evidence-tracking mechanisms, not just better priors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hallucination is widely acknowledged, but a controlled scaling study of hallucination severity in restoration may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or collect a capacity ladder of one restoration family, build an ambiguous-input evaluation set with known ground truth, and measure semantic error and plausibility versus scale.
main_risk: Semantic error annotation is labor-intensive and ambiguity levels must be carefully controlled for the trend to be interpretable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better generative models are expected to hallucinate less because they know more about the world.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where evidence is absent, the posterior is prior-dominated by definition; a stronger prior samples sharper, more convincing content, but the true content is unrecoverable, so conviction rises while accuracy cannot.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore identical barely-legible text crops with a weak and a strong public generative restorer and count legible-but-wrong outputs; more confident wrong text from the stronger model is the predicted signature.

one_line_idea: Face restoration homogenizes identity, drifting restored faces toward the training distribution's typical attributes, measurable as systematic embedding shift.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Face restoration models are trained on face datasets with specific demographic and photographic compositions, and severe degradation leaves identity underdetermined.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Restored faces exhibit a consistent drift in identity-embedding space toward dense regions of the training distribution, so restoration reduces inter-identity variance and biases perceived attributes toward the training majority.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Embedding distances between restored faces and their true identities will show a directional bias toward training-set attribute centroids, growing with degradation severity, and inter-identity embedding variance will shrink after restoration.
why_important: Identity distortion in face restoration has fairness, forensic, and personal-dignity implications, and the effect is invisible to standard quality metrics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Identity preservation is measured as similarity to ground truth, but characterizing the direction of identity error as distribution-seeking drift may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Degrade faces of known identities at increasing severity, restore, compute identity embeddings, and test for directional drift toward training centroids and variance shrinkage.
main_risk: Face embedding models have their own biases, which must be controlled to avoid measuring the auditor instead of the restorer.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Identity errors in face restoration are assumed to be unbiased noise around the true identity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Under ambiguity, optimal samplers draw from the prior's dense regions; the prior is the training distribution, so errors must be systematically distribution-seeking rather than isotropic.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore heavily degraded faces of a few individuals with a public face restorer many times, average the embeddings, and check whether averaged restorations move consistently toward a common direction rather than scattering around the true identity.

one_line_idea: Restoration models should abstain on illegible text instead of fabricating legible wrong characters, and text-aware abstention is implementable without hurting non-text quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative restorers render crisp, legible characters even when input text is information-theoretically unreadable, producing convincing but wrong words.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A text-region-aware restoration policy that preserves illegibility (or marks uncertainty) when character evidence is insufficient eliminates most harmful text hallucination at negligible cost to overall perceptual quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The abstaining model will show a large reduction in legible-but-incorrect text outputs compared to standard models, with no significant preference loss on images without text.
why_important: Fabricated text is among the most consequential restoration failures (documents, signage, evidence), and it is fixable by policy rather than by better priors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Text-prior-equipped restorers aim to guess better; an explicit abstention formulation for restoration may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a restorer with a text-detection branch and an abstention objective in text regions below an evidence threshold, then measure wrong-legible-text rates and global preference against baselines.
main_risk: Calibrating the evidence threshold is hard; over-abstention would preserve blur that users dislike.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Sharper text output is treated as strictly better, with correctness assumed to follow from stronger text priors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For genuinely unreadable input, no prior recovers the true string; every legible rendering is a guess, and presenting guesses as recovered fact is a design flaw rather than a capability gap.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run popular restorers on synthetically blurred text below a legibility threshold and count how often outputs are confidently legible and wrong; a high rate motivates the abstention policy immediately.

one_line_idea: Late-stage sampling in diffusion-based SR is only weakly conditioned on the input, so the fine detail users see is mostly prior draw rather than evidence.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Diffusion restorers inject conditioning throughout the sampling trajectory, but the influence of conditioning on each stage of synthesis is not routinely measured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dependence of the output on the degraded input is concentrated in early, coarse-structure sampling stages, while late stages that synthesize fine texture are close to unconditional, meaning the visible detail is largely input-independent.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Swapping the conditioning image mid-trajectory will change coarse layout only when swapped early, and late-trajectory swaps will leave outputs nearly unchanged, demonstrating vanishing late-stage conditioning influence.
why_important: If fine detail is essentially unconditional, diffusion SR is texture synthesis with an evidence-shaped scaffold, which should change how it is evaluated and disclosed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Trajectory-stage analyses exist for generation, but quantifying stage-wise conditioning influence specifically for restoration fidelity may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Perform conditioning-swap and conditioning-ablation interventions at controlled trajectory points across many images, and measure output sensitivity as a function of intervention time.
main_risk: Results may vary across samplers and guidance mechanisms, requiring a broad matrix to generalize.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Conditioning is assumed to constrain synthesis uniformly through the trajectory.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-resolution evidence constrains low frequencies; once coarse structure is fixed, the remaining synthesis is dominated by the prior because the evidence has no high-frequency content to contribute.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one public diffusion restorer, swap the conditioning image at a late sampling step and observe whether the output detail changes; near-identical outputs confirm weak late-stage conditioning within minutes.

one_line_idea: Sample diversity in stochastic restoration is misallocated: seeds vary irrelevant texture while collapsing on semantically ambiguous content where diversity actually matters.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Stochastic restorers advertise multiple plausible outputs as a feature representing posterior uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-seed variation concentrates in perceptually irrelevant micro-texture while semantically ambiguous regions (which face, which character) collapse to a single mode, so the advertised diversity does not represent the true posterior where it counts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing cross-seed variance into semantic and textural components will show textural variance dominating by a large factor, and constructed inputs with genuinely multimodal semantic posteriors will yield single-mode outputs across seeds.
why_important: Users interpreting sample spread as uncertainty will be misled precisely on high-stakes ambiguous content.
