minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a restoration model with a differentiable compression proxy in the loss, then compare against standard models on human preference after real platform-grade re-compression.
main_risk: Platform compression parameters vary and change over time, making the target moving and partially unknown.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration quality is assumed to be preserved proportionally by downstream compression, leaving rankings intact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Compression allocates bits by signal statistics; synthesized stochastic texture is expensive to encode and gets destroyed first, so the ranking before and after compression cannot generally coincide.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-compress outputs of a perceptual and a fidelity model at platform-typical quality and compare which degrades more visibly; a reversal of visual advantage after compression on sample images is quick evidence.

one_line_idea: Restoration models entangle tone and color enhancement with structural restoration, and disentangling shows part of perceived restoration quality is uncredited color grading.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Trained restorers change color statistics and tone curves alongside structure, since training pairs and losses do not separate the two.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable share of human preference for outputs of modern restorers is attributable to incidental tone and color changes rather than structural recovery, and factoring outputs into color transform plus structural change reveals models differ far less structurally than leaderboards suggest.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying each model's global color-tone transform to a common structural baseline will recover a substantial fraction of the preference gap between models, showing color grading contributes materially to perceived ranking.
why_important: If part of the measured progress is color grading, structure-focused research claims are overcredited, and fair comparisons require color-normalized evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Color shifts are noted as artifacts, but decomposing preference gains into grading and structure components may be unattempted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit global or local color transforms mapping each model's outputs from a common baseline, run preference studies on color-matched outputs, and compare gaps before and after normalization.
main_risk: Color and structure interact perceptually, so a clean decomposition may be only approximately achievable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Preference differences between restorers are read as structural quality differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tone and saturation shifts reliably move human preference on their own, and nothing in current training prevents models from exploiting this channel; unmeasured channels get exploited.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Histogram-match outputs of two competing models to identical color statistics and rerun a small preference test; a shrunken gap after matching demonstrates the grading contribution.

one_line_idea: Warped-frame temporal consistency metrics reward temporally stable hallucination over faithful but variable detail, making them anti-fidelity in exactly the hard cases.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Video restoration papers report temporal consistency via warped-frame differences, penalizing any detail change between aligned frames.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] These metrics assign better scores to a model that hallucinates the same wrong detail consistently than to one that renders correct detail with slight temporal variation, so optimizing them steers video restorers toward stable fabrication.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructed output pairs (consistent-wrong versus variable-right) will show the consistency metric preferring consistent-wrong, and models tuned for the metric will exhibit increased persistent hallucination measured against ground truth.
why_important: Temporal consistency is the headline metric of video restoration; if it rewards locked-in fabrication, the subfield optimizes an anti-goal.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The blur-versus-flicker tension is known; formalizing the consistent-hallucination failure of warping metrics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build controlled output sequences varying correctness and temporal stability independently, score them with standard consistency metrics, and map the metric's preference structure against fidelity.
main_risk: Optical-flow errors in metric computation add noise that complicates clean attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher temporal consistency is assumed to be monotonically better for video restoration quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Consistency measures agreement with the model's own past output, not with reality; self-agreement is trivially maximized by committing to any fixed content, right or wrong.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Score a deliberately frozen-detail (wrong but stable) rendering against a lightly flickering faithful rendering of one clip with a standard consistency metric; the metric preferring the frozen fabrication proves the point on one example.

one_line_idea: The multi-frame advantage of video SR collapses on properly anti-aliased or heavily compressed footage, because models exploit temporal aliasing as their main cross-frame cue.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Video SR is assumed to beat single-image SR by aggregating sub-pixel information across frames, and benchmarks typically use synthetically downsampled clips whose resampling preserves aliasing.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Much of the measured multi-frame gain comes from aliasing patterns that shift predictably with motion; on anti-aliased or codec-smoothed footage, the recoverable cross-frame signal shrinks and video SR degrades toward per-frame SR quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The gap between video SR and single-frame SR will shrink markedly as anti-aliasing strength or compression level of the source increases, holding content and motion fixed.
why_important: It defines when multi-frame processing is worth its cost, and suggests benchmark resampling choices have overstated practical video SR value.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Aliasing's role in classical multi-frame SR theory is known, but quantifying how much modern learned video SR depends on it across realistic acquisition conditions may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct matched clip sets with graded anti-aliasing and compression, evaluate video SR and single-frame baselines on each, and plot the multi-frame gain against source treatment.
main_risk: Codec temporal processing introduces its own cross-frame structure, complicating the attribution to aliasing alone.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multi-frame aggregation is assumed to deliver robust gains whenever motion is present.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Classical sampling theory ties multi-frame recoverability to aliased residual signal; remove the aliasing and the extra frames carry mostly redundant low-pass information.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one public video SR model on the same clip downsampled with and without strong anti-aliasing and compare its margin over a single-frame model; margin collapse on the anti-aliased clip is quick evidence.

one_line_idea: Codec-informed video restoration using bitstream metadata (block boundaries, motion vectors, quantization levels) beats blind pixel-space restoration at equal capacity, and discarding the bitstream is an unforced error.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Compressed video arrives with rich structural metadata in the bitstream, yet most learned video restoration decodes to pixels and discards everything else.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Codec artifacts are deterministic functions of encoding decisions recoverable from the bitstream, so conditioning restoration on bitstream metadata resolves artifact-versus-content ambiguity that pixel-only models must guess, yielding consistent quality gains especially at low bitrates.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A metadata-conditioned model will outperform a matched pixel-only model on compressed-video restoration, with the gain growing as bitrate decreases and artifact ambiguity rises.
why_important: Compressed video is the dominant video restoration workload; a free conditioning signal that resolves its central ambiguity would shift practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Bitstream-aware enhancement exists in codec-specific niches; a general audit of how much blind pixel-space restoration loses by ignoring the bitstream may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Encode a corpus at multiple bitrates, train matched models with and without bitstream conditioning, and compare quality across bitrates and artifact types.
main_risk: Bitstream access is lost when video is re-encoded or re-containered by platforms, limiting applicability to first-decode scenarios.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Pixel-space learning is assumed to recover whatever the bitstream would have told the model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Distinguishing a blocking artifact from a real edge at a block boundary is ambiguous in pixels but trivially resolved by knowing the boundary and its quantization step; ambiguity resolution is information the pixels alone lack.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Provide a restoration model oracle block-boundary and quantization maps as extra channels on a small compressed set and measure the gain; a clear improvement establishes the value of bitstream information cheaply.

one_line_idea: Recurrent video restorers accumulate hallucination drift over long sequences, diverging from input content in ways short-clip benchmarks never measure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Recurrent and propagation-based video restorers carry state across frames, and standard benchmarks evaluate on clips of at most a few seconds.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Propagated state accretes synthesized detail that recursively conditions later frames, so over hundreds of frames outputs drift measurably away from evidence (texture lock-in, progressive stylization), a failure invisible at benchmark clip lengths.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evidence-consistency error will grow with sequence position for recurrent models on long clips while remaining flat for per-frame models, and periodic state resets will trade drift reduction against temporal smoothness.
why_important: Real workloads (film restoration, surveillance archives) run for hours; a drift failure mode invalidates long-content deployment of recurrent designs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Error accumulation is studied in video prediction; hallucination drift audits for recurrent restoration may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run recurrent restorers on long synthetic sequences with ground truth, plot fidelity and consistency metrics against frame index, and compare with per-frame baselines and reset schedules.
main_risk: Drift may be model-specific and small for well-regularized designs, making the general claim depend on the model panel.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Recurrent propagation is assumed to add information without compounding risk, since each frame provides fresh evidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The state mixes evidence with synthesis, and later frames cannot distinguish the two; feeding synthesis back as if it were evidence is a textbook positive-feedback loop.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one public recurrent model on a long static-camera clip and difference early and late outputs of identical content; growing divergence of stable content across time reveals drift directly.

one_line_idea: Short-clip training gives recurrent video restorers an implicit state-reset bias, making their effective temporal receptive field far shorter than architecture diagrams claim.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Recurrent video restorers are trained on short clips for memory reasons, then deployed on long sequences under the assumption that recurrence accumulates information indefinitely.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training on short clips teaches the recurrence to discount information beyond the training-clip horizon, so the effective temporal receptive field saturates near the training length and additional context frames at inference contribute nearly nothing.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Occluding or corrupting frames at increasing temporal distance from the target frame will show influence decaying sharply around the training clip length across recurrent models, regardless of architectural memory capacity.
why_important: If effective memory is training-bounded, claims of long-range aggregation are wrong, and training-schedule changes (longer clips, truncated-backprop curricula) matter more than architecture.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Effective receptive fields are measured for spatial CNNs; the temporal analogue for learned video restoration may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure temporal influence functions (output sensitivity to controlled perturbations at varying frame offsets) for models trained with different clip lengths, and locate the influence horizon relative to training length.
main_risk: Influence measurement interacts with scene motion, requiring motion-controlled synthetic sequences for clean curves.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Recurrent architectures are assumed to integrate evidence over arbitrarily long horizons at inference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gradients never rewarded remembering beyond the clip during training, and unrewarded capacity decays to whatever behavior minimizes short-clip loss, which is forgetting.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Feed one public recurrent model the same target frame with progressively longer real context prefixes and measure output change; a plateau at short prefix lengths exposes the bounded memory quickly.

one_line_idea: Face-video enhancement alters lip and expression micro-motion, measurably changing perceived speech and emotion, a safety-relevant failure invisible to every current metric.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Video enhancement is routinely applied to talking-head footage (conferencing, archival interviews, journalism), and facial micro-motion carries communicative content.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Generative video enhancement modifies mouth shapes and micro-expressions enough to change lip-reading interpretation and perceived affect in a measurable fraction of clips, meaning enhancement can alter the communicative record while passing all quality metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Lip-reading systems and human judges will disagree more with original footage after enhancement than metric-matched traditional processing predicts, with disagreement concentrated in low-quality source regions where the prior dominates.
why_important: Altering what a person appears to say or feel is a qualitatively severe harm for journalism, evidence, and archives, and no current evaluation practice would detect it.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Lip-sync generation is studied for synthesis; auditing unintended communicative alteration by enhancement models may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Enhance degraded talking-head clips with generative video models, run automatic lip-reading and human perception panels on original versus enhanced, and quantify interpretation shifts.
main_risk: Lip-reading systems are imperfect, so human panels are required for load-bearing conclusions, raising study cost.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Enhancement is assumed to change appearance quality while leaving communicative content untouched.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mouth regions are small, fast-moving, and often degraded, exactly where generative priors take over; the prior encodes typical mouth motion, not this speaker's actual utterance.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Enhance a few low-quality clips of known speech and check whether visible mouth shapes still match the transcript frame-by-frame; discovered mismatches on a small sample establish the phenomenon.

one_line_idea: Video restoration allocates compute suboptimally across frames: temporal information saturates after a few neighbors, and reallocating compute to per-frame quality dominates at fixed budget.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Video restoration architectures differ widely in how many frames they ingest and how much compute each frame receives, with the frame window treated as an architectural given rather than an optimized budget split.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The marginal value of additional context frames decays fast (most recoverable cross-frame information lives in the nearest few frames), so at a fixed FLOP budget, small-window models with stronger per-frame processing beat wide-window models with thinner processing.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An iso-FLOP sweep across window-size and per-frame-capacity combinations will show the quality optimum at small windows for most degradation types, with wide windows winning only under severe noise where temporal averaging dominates.
why_important: It provides a principled budget rule for practical video restoration design instead of unexamined window conventions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ablations of frame windows exist per paper, but a systematic iso-compute frontier across the window-capacity plane may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a model family over a grid of window sizes and per-frame capacities at matched total FLOPs, evaluate across degradation types, and map the iso-compute quality frontier.
main_risk: Conclusions may depend on motion statistics of the evaluation corpus, requiring motion-stratified reporting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More temporal context is assumed to be worth its compute cost whenever available.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Alignment error grows with temporal distance, so far frames contribute noisy, misregistered evidence whose value can be negative; the useful information is concentrated where alignment is reliable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one flexible public model with progressively truncated frame windows and measure quality; an early plateau in the quality-versus-window curve indicates fast temporal saturation.

one_line_idea: Synthetic video SR benchmarks miss the coupling between motion blur, shutter time, and frame rate in real capture, and this coupling breaks synthetic-to-real transfer more than spatial degradation mismatch.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic video benchmarks downsample sharp source frames spatially, while real capture couples temporal integration (motion blur proportional to shutter time) with frame rate and exposure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on spatially-degraded-but-temporally-sharp frames misinterpret real motion blur as spatial blur, applying wrong corrections along motion trajectories, and adding physically coupled temporal blur synthesis to training closes more of the real-video gap than improving spatial degradation realism.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On real footage with natural motion blur, models trained with coupled spatio-temporal degradation will beat spatial-only models by a larger margin than any spatial-realism upgrade achieves, with gains concentrated on moving content.
why_important: It identifies the dominant missing axis of video degradation modeling, redirecting benchmark construction and training synthesis.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Motion blur synthesis exists in deblurring; ranking temporal-coupling realism against spatial realism as transfer factors for video SR may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build training variants isolating spatial realism and temporal-coupling realism, train matched models, and evaluate on real captured footage stratified by motion magnitude.
main_risk: Ground truth for real moving content is hard to obtain, pushing evaluation toward no-reference or staged-capture protocols.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Spatial degradation realism is treated as the main lever for closing the synthetic-to-real video gap.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporal integration is a physically mandatory component of every real exposure; a training distribution with zero temporal blur is wrong about every moving pixel in every real video.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a spatial-only-trained video SR model on footage with strong motion blur and inspect moving-object treatment against static regions; systematic mishandling of motion-blurred content is visible on a few clips.

one_line_idea: Restore-then-recognize pipelines lose to recognition models trained directly on degraded inputs, because restoration destroys machine-relevant evidence while adding human-pleasing detail.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners insert restoration models before recognition systems on low-quality imagery, assuming visual improvement implies recognition improvement.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Restoration is a lossy, prior-injecting transform of the evidence; degradation-adapted recognition preserves task-relevant information better, so restore-then-recognize underperforms degraded-input fine-tuning at matched effort across common tasks and severities.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across detection and recognition tasks under matched adaptation budgets, degraded-trained recognizers will beat pipelines using pretrained restorers, with the pipeline deficit growing as restoration becomes more generative.
why_important: The restore-first pattern is deployed widely; if it is systematically inferior, substantial deployed compute produces negative value for machine consumers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Task-driven restoration papers exist with mixed findings; a comprehensive matched-budget comparison across the modern generative restoration regime may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix tasks and degradations, compare degraded-finetuned recognizers against restore-then-recognize with equal adaptation compute, sweeping restoration operating points from fidelity to perceptual.
main_risk: Results may reverse in the extreme-degradation regime where recognizers fail outright, requiring severity-stratified claims.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better-looking inputs are assumed to yield better recognition, making restoration a safe preprocessing default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recognition needs likelihood-relevant evidence, and restoration replaces ambiguous evidence with confident prior samples; the replacement is exactly the information a recognizer would have weighed differently.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare a pretrained detector on degraded images against the same detector on restored versions of them; observing restoration-induced accuracy drops on a sample already contradicts the safe-default assumption.

one_line_idea: Generative restoration invalidates images as evidence, and restoration systems for forensic contexts should emit per-region fidelity certificates grounded in observation consistency.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Enhanced images circulate in investigative, legal, and journalistic contexts, while generative restorers can fabricate exactly the details (plates, faces, text) such contexts care about.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A certification layer that decomposes each output region into evidence-supported and prior-injected components, with quantified consistency bounds under the estimated forward model, can be attached to restoration outputs and would change downstream trust decisions in measurable ways.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Certificates validated on synthetic cases will correctly flag most fabricated regions, and user studies with investigators will show materially different reliance decisions when certificates are shown.
why_important: Society is consuming restored imagery as if it were evidence; an auditable fidelity standard is the difference between a tool and a hazard in these settings.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Uncertainty maps exist in research; an operational certification framework tied to forward-model consistency for forensic consumption may be unbuilt.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define certificate semantics, implement estimation from consistency residuals and sampling dispersion, validate flagging accuracy on synthetic ground truth, and run a decision study with professional users.
main_risk: Certificates could confer unjustified authority if their own error rates are misunderstood, requiring careful calibration reporting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration quality is treated as a single scalar, with evidentiary reliability considered outside the field's scope.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information needed for certification (forward-model residuals, posterior dispersion) already exists inside restoration pipelines; discarding it is a choice, not a necessity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Prototype certificates from cross-seed variance plus re-degradation residuals on synthetic forensic-style cases (plates, documents) and measure how often flagged regions coincide with actual fabrications.

one_line_idea: Natural-photo priors contaminate scientific imagery: restoration models trained on photographs inject natural-image statistics into scientific data, creating plausible artifacts that could mislead analysis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Off-the-shelf restoration and SR tools trained on natural photographs are applied to scientific imagery (microscopy, astronomy, remote sensing style data) whose statistics differ fundamentally from photographs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Photo-trained restorers systematically reshape scientific image content toward natural-image statistics (edge sharpening, texture regularization, structure completion), producing artifacts that domain experts judge plausible but that alter quantitative measurements derived from the images.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On synthetic scientific-style data with known ground truth, photo-trained restoration will bias derived measurements (object counts, boundary positions, intensity profiles) in consistent directions, while domain-matched restorers will not.
why_important: Scientific conclusions downstream of contaminated images inherit the bias invisibly; the failure mode deserves a name and a measurement protocol before it deserves a fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Domain shift is acknowledged, but framing prior contamination as a measurable bias on downstream scientific measurements may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synthetic data with controlled ground-truth structure mimicking scientific imaging statistics, restore with photo-trained models, and quantify measurement bias against domain-matched baselines.
main_risk: Synthetic scientific data may not capture real instrument statistics, limiting external validity of the bias estimates.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration tools are assumed domain-agnostic enough that visible improvement implies measurement safety.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The prior is the training distribution; applying it to data from a different distribution mathematically biases the posterior toward photograph statistics, and the bias lands on whatever quantities the analysis measures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore a synthetic point-source field (astronomy-like) with a photo-trained SR model and measure source positions and fluxes before and after; systematic shifts on this one construction demonstrate contamination.

one_line_idea: In safety-critical imaging, hallucination concentrates on exactly the fine structures that matter most, and abstention-based restoration (enhance only what evidence supports) is the correct product for these domains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration tools are marketed toward safety-adjacent uses (document recovery, identification, clinical-adjacent imaging), where decisions hinge on fine structures near the resolution limit.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The structures that drive decisions in such domains (thin lines, small lesions-like marks, character strokes, serial numbers) are precisely the evidence-poor high-frequency content that generative restorers fill from the prior, so hallucination probability is highest exactly where decision weight is highest, and an abstention-based design dominates on decision-quality metrics despite losing on image-quality metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying synthetic evaluations by decision-relevance of regions will show hallucination rates rising with decision weight for standard restorers, and abstaining restorers will yield better downstream decision accuracy despite worse perceptual scores.
why_important: It formalizes why perceptual quality is the wrong objective for safety-critical restoration and offers a concrete alternative design target.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Selective prediction is standard in classification; abstention as a first-class restoration output mode may be undeveloped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct decision tasks on synthetic imagery with degradation, compare standard and abstention-based restoration on downstream decision accuracy and calibration of the abstention masks.
main_risk: Abstention masks must themselves be reliable; a miscalibrated abstainer could be worse than an honest disclaimer on the whole image.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher perceptual restoration quality is assumed to help any downstream decision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decision-relevant structures are rare, small, and near the information floor; the prior has maximal freedom there, and maximal freedom under a realism objective means confident invention.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Degrade images containing small decision-critical marks until marginally detectable, restore with a generative model, and measure how often marks are removed, moved, or invented; error concentration on the marks confirms the alignment of hallucination with decision weight.

one_line_idea: Restoration-as-decoder compression schemes (send low quality, restore at receiver) are evaluated with perceptual metrics that hide semantic drift, and round-trip semantic audits would cap their claimed bitrate savings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Neural compression proposals use restoration or generation at the decoder to reconstruct from aggressive compression, reporting strong perceptual quality at low bitrates.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At the advertised low bitrates, decoder-side generation alters semantic content (object identity details, text, counts) at rates that perceptual and distributional metrics do not register, and a semantic round-trip audit (does the reconstruction preserve task-relevant facts) would show the effective safe bitrate is substantially higher than claimed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Semantic-consistency measures between source and reconstruction will degrade sharply below a bitrate threshold while perceptual metrics stay flat, revealing a hidden semantic cliff in generative compression.
why_important: Compression standards affect all stored imagery; adopting perceptual-metric-validated generative codecs without semantic audits risks institutionalizing content alteration.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Generative codecs are evaluated on realism and distortion; standardized semantic-preservation audits across bitrates may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run generative and traditional codecs across bitrate ladders, evaluate semantic preservation via recognition, text, and counting probes, and locate the semantic cliff relative to perceptual metric behavior.
main_risk: Semantic probes cover finite aspects; passing the audit does not certify full semantic preservation, only bounded aspects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Perceptual quality at matched bitrate is treated as the sufficient criterion for codec superiority.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Below some bitrate the decoder must synthesize most content from the prior; synthesis preserves style before facts, and only fact-sensitive probes can see the difference.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compress text-bearing and face-bearing images with one generative codec at aggressive settings and check fact preservation (readable strings, identity) against the source; semantic alterations at flat perceptual scores make the case.

one_line_idea: Human-optimal and OCR-optimal restorations of degraded text diverge: images that read best to machines look worse to humans, motivating task-conditional restoration outputs.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Degraded documents are restored both for human reading and for OCR pipelines, using the same models tuned for visual quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The restoration operating point maximizing OCR accuracy differs systematically from the one maximizing human preference (OCR benefits from stroke-preserving, contrast-exaggerated, ligature-conservative renderings humans find ugly), so a single output is suboptimal for both consumers and models should emit task-conditioned variants.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping restoration operating points on degraded documents will produce OCR-accuracy and human-preference curves peaking at different points, with a measurable accuracy sacrifice at the human-preferred point.
why_important: Document pipelines silently choose one point for both audiences; knowing the divergence lets systems serve each consumer its optimum.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Task-driven restoration is known in principle; mapping the human-machine divergence specifically for document restoration operating points may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Restore degraded documents across an operating-point sweep, measure OCR accuracy with standard engines and human preference with reading panels, and compare peak locations.
main_risk: Divergence size may depend on the OCR engine generation, with modern engines potentially more tolerant of human-preferred renderings.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restoration that helps humans read is assumed to help machines read comparably.
why_it_might_be_wrong: OCR decisions depend on features (stroke topology, binarization stability) that differ from human aesthetic drivers (smoothness, naturalness); optimizing one has no reason to optimize the other.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare OCR error rates on a perceptually restored versus an aggressively contrast-enhanced ugly restoration of the same degraded pages; the ugly variant winning on OCR while losing on looks demonstrates the divergence.

one_line_idea: For machine consumption, restoring feature embeddings directly beats restoring pixels first: pixel space is a human-oriented bottleneck that wastes capacity on visually pleasing but task-irrelevant detail.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Machine pipelines that analyze degraded imagery typically restore to pixels first, then extract features, even when no human views the intermediate image.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Learning a degraded-to-clean mapping directly in the feature space of the downstream model preserves task information better and costs less than pixel restoration, because pixel realism constraints are irrelevant to the consumer and actively divert capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Feature-space restoration will match or beat pixel-restoration pipelines on downstream accuracy across degradation severities at a fraction of the compute, with the advantage largest under severe degradation where pixel realism is most expensive.
why_important: A large share of restoration compute worldwide serves machine-only pipelines; removing the pixel detour would be a structural efficiency and accuracy win.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Feature-level robustness techniques exist; framing restoration itself as a feature-space task with systematic comparison against pixel pipelines may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train feature-space restorers for fixed downstream models across degradations, compare accuracy and compute against restore-then-extract pipelines with matched adaptation budgets.
main_risk: Feature-space restorers are consumer-specific, losing the reusability of a pixel image across multiple downstream tasks.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The pixel image is treated as the natural universal interface between restoration and any downstream use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The downstream task defines sufficient statistics; reconstructing all pixels reconstructs mostly nuisance dimensions, and the nuisance reconstruction is where generative restoration spends most of its effort.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a small adapter mapping degraded-image features to clean-image features for one frozen recognizer and compare downstream accuracy against a public restorer feeding the same recognizer; a quick win for the adapter on one task motivates the full study.

one_line_idea: Face enhancement shifts identity-verification scores asymmetrically across demographic groups, so restoration can silently change biometric outcomes with disparate impact.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Enhanced or restored face images are fed into verification and identification systems in consumer and institutional settings, and face restoration training data has demographic composition biases.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Restoration-induced changes to identity-embedding similarity are not demographically uniform: groups underrepresented in restoration training data experience larger and more variable similarity shifts, measurably changing false-match and false-non-match behavior after enhancement.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Demographic stratification of pre-versus-post-enhancement verification score shifts will show significant group differences in shift magnitude and direction, with effect size tracking training-data representation.
why_important: Biometric decisions carry legal weight; an enhancement step that moves error rates differently per group is a concrete, auditable fairness hazard hiding inside an innocuous-looking preprocessing stage.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Recognition bias is studied, and restoration bias is studied for quality; the coupling (restoration-induced biometric score shifts per group) may be unaudited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Degrade and restore identity-labeled face sets with demographic annotations, run standard verification systems, and compare score-shift distributions per group against matched controls.
main_risk: Verification systems have their own demographic biases, requiring careful separation of restorer-induced from recognizer-induced effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Enhancement is assumed neutral for verification, either helping all groups or degrading all groups similarly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Under ambiguity the restorer pulls faces toward its training density; the pull direction and strength depend on where the subject sits relative to that density, which is what demographic representation determines.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Enhance a demographically stratified degraded face sample with one public face restorer and measure verification score shifts per group against originals; visible asymmetry on a modest sample flags the hazard.

one_line_idea: Most claimed architecture gains in SR are training-recipe gains: under matched modern recipes, a decade of architectural innovations compresses into a much smaller quality spread than the literature implies.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Each SR architecture generation was published with its own training data, augmentation, schedule, and loss configuration, and improvements were attributed to architecture.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Retraining historical SR architectures under one modern shared recipe will compress inter-architecture differences dramatically, showing that much of the reported progression reflects recipe evolution rather than architectural superiority.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The quality spread across retrained historical architectures will shrink to a fraction of the published spread, with some old architectures matching much newer ones under equal recipes.
why_important: It recalibrates what the field actually learned about architecture and redirects credit and future effort toward the recipe components that mattered.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Recipe-controlled re-evaluations exist in classification; an equivalent systematic audit for the SR architecture lineage may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select architectures spanning the SR lineage, retrain all under one strong shared recipe at matched compute, and compare the resulting spread against the published record.
main_risk: A single shared recipe may favor some architecture families, requiring per-family recipe tuning to bound the fairness objection.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The published SR quality progression is read as a history of architectural insight.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recipes improved simultaneously with architectures and were never held constant; entangled factors mean the attribution to architecture was never actually measured.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Retrain one early architecture with a modern recipe and compare it against a recent model's published numbers; a surprising catch-up on this single data point justifies the full audit.

one_line_idea: SR models are not scale-consistent (twice 2x differs from once 4x), and enforcing scale-composition consistency at training improves generalization to unseen scales for free.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SR models are trained per scale factor or with scale conditioning, and nothing in standard training constrains compositions of small-factor applications to agree with single large-factor applications.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The divergence between composed and direct upscaling is large and systematic (composition amplifies each stage's biases), and adding a composition-consistency loss both shrinks the divergence and improves quality at scales never seen in training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measured composition gaps will be substantial for standard models, and consistency-trained models will show smaller gaps plus better interpolation and extrapolation across the scale axis at matched capacity.
why_important: Scale consistency is a structural sanity property; exploiting it is a free regularizer and its violation is an interpretable diagnostic of learned operator quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Arbitrary-scale architectures exist, but composition-consistency as an explicit training constraint and diagnostic may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantify composition gaps across public models, then train matched models with and without a composition-consistency objective and evaluate on seen and unseen scales.
main_risk: Consistency could be achieved by making all paths equally mediocre, so quality metrics must accompany the gap metric.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-scale performance is optimized independently, with cross-scale coherence assumed irrelevant to quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The true continuous imaging operator family is self-consistent under composition; a learned family violating this is provably wrong somewhere, and the violation energy is trainable signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Apply one public 2x model twice and its 4x sibling once to the same inputs and difference the results; large structured disagreement on the first images quantifies the inconsistency immediately.

one_line_idea: Small-crop training biases SR models against global structure: long edges, vanishing lines, and large-scale gradients are reconstructed with systematic errors that large-context training fixes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] SR models train on small crops for throughput, and evaluation crops are similarly small, so neither training nor evaluation exercises structures larger than the crop.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Crop-bounded training leaves models unable to maintain global geometric coherence (straightness of long edges, perspective-consistent texture gradients, smooth large-area shading), producing measurable structure errors on full images that crop-based metrics never see, and training with larger context repairs them at modest cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Purpose-built global-structure metrics (long-edge straightness, gradient smoothness across the frame) will reveal systematic errors in crop-trained models that decrease monotonically with training context size.
why_important: Full images are the product; a structural error family invisible to the field's measurement loop can persist indefinitely without being noticed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Receptive-field discussion exists; connecting crop-size training policy to a measurable global-structure error family in SR may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models across a crop-size ladder, define and validate global-structure metrics on full-image evaluations, and map error against training context size.
main_risk: Global-structure metrics are new instruments needing their own validation against human judgment of structural fidelity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Local restoration quality is assumed to compose into global quality automatically.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Straightness and perspective coherence are constraints spanning distances the crop-trained model has never processed as a unit; nothing in its training distribution enforces them.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Restore images with long architectural edges using a standard model and measure edge deviation from fitted lines; consistent waviness beyond input levels shows the failure family exists.

one_line_idea: SR models get amplitude spectra roughly right but phase systematically wrong, and phase error is the better predictor of perceived structural artifacts, motivating phase-aware losses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration losses operate pointwise or on learned features, without explicit control over how reconstruction error distributes between spectral amplitude and phase, while phase is known to carry structural information in images.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Trained SR models allocate error disproportionately to phase in high frequencies (plausible energy, misplaced structure), phase error correlates with human-perceived structural artifacts better than amplitude error, and adding an explicit phase-coherence term to training reduces structural artifacts at equal amplitude accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Spectral decomposition of errors across models will show phase-dominated high-frequency error, human artifact ratings will track phase error more than amplitude error, and phase-regularized training will improve artifact ratings.
why_important: It offers a physically interpretable account of what perceptual losses vaguely address, and a targeted, cheap loss ingredient.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spectral analyses of GAN artifacts exist; a phase-centric error accounting and phase-targeted loss for SR may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Decompose reconstruction errors of a model panel into amplitude and phase components per band, collect artifact ratings, correlate, then train matched models with and without phase terms.
main_risk: Global Fourier phase is a crude descriptor for local structure, and windowed analyses add parameter choices that affect conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Spectral amplitude realism is treated as the main frequency-domain target, with phase left implicit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pointwise losses are minimized by hedging phase where uncertain, and adversarial losses enforce marginal statistics that constrain amplitude much more than phase alignment with the source.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Swap the phase of model outputs with ground-truth phase (keeping model amplitude) on a few images; a dramatic perceived-quality jump from ground-truth phase alone demonstrates phase is the binding error.

one_line_idea: Restoration data scaling hits diminishing returns quickly on content diversity but not on degradation diversity, so data budgets should buy degradations, not images.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Restoration training sets are scaled by adding more images, following the generation-and-recognition intuition that content scale drives capability.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Restoration quality saturates rapidly with content count at fixed degradation coverage, while it keeps improving with degradation-distribution enrichment at fixed content, because the learned inverse operator depends more on degradation coverage than on content memorization.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An iso-budget grid over content count and degradation richness will show quality iso-lines running nearly parallel to the content axis beyond a modest content threshold, with degradation richness dominating the gradient.
why_important: It gives a concrete data-collection policy (invest in degradation realism and coverage) that contradicts the default more-images instinct, saving large data costs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-scaling studies exist for recognition and generation; a two-axis content-versus-degradation scaling law for restoration may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models across a factorial grid of content-set sizes and degradation-distribution richness levels, and fit quality surfaces over the two axes.
main_risk: The result may depend on the perceptual-versus-fidelity operating point, since texture-synthesis quality may keep benefiting from content scale.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More training images are assumed to be the reliable path to better restoration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The inverse operator must generalize over degradations at test time, not over unseen content statistics, which natural images share broadly; the binding generalization axis is the one benchmarks vary least.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train two small models, one on few images with rich degradations and one on many images with a narrow pipeline, at equal compute, and compare on out-of-pipeline degradations; the few-images model winning would flip the default instinct.

one_line_idea: SR models collapse rare textures onto common ones: outputs re-render unusual materials as the nearest frequent texture family, a measurable prior-collapse effect invisible to aggregate metrics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Natural texture frequency is heavy-tailed in training corpora, and SR models synthesize texture under ambiguity using what they learned from that skewed distribution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under degradation-induced ambiguity, models systematically substitute rare textures (unusual fabrics, materials, biological structures) with high-frequency common textures, and texture-classification of outputs versus ground truth will reveal directional substitution toward head classes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A texture-classifier audit of restored outputs will show tail-class recall dropping far more than head-class recall as degradation increases, with substitutions flowing tail-to-head rather than randomly.
why_important: Texture identity carries semantic content (material, condition, authenticity); silent substitution toward common textures is misinformation for any use that reads material properties from images.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Long-tail effects are studied in recognition; a directional texture-substitution audit for restoration may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a texture-labeled evaluation set spanning frequency tiers, degrade and restore, classify output textures, and measure the substitution flow matrix across tiers and severities.
main_risk: Texture classification of synthesized outputs is itself fallible, so human verification of substitution cases is needed for load-bearing claims.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Texture synthesis errors are assumed to be quality degradations rather than directional identity substitutions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Posterior sampling under an imbalanced prior mathematically favors head classes when evidence is weak; the substitution direction is a theorem-shaped consequence, not an accident.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Degrade and restore close-ups of a few unusual materials and ask raters what material the output shows; consistent misreading toward common materials demonstrates the collapse on a handful of cases.

one_line_idea: Blind training over mixed severities teaches models a severity-averaged inverse that is wrong for every severity, and cheap explicit severity conditioning dominates blind averaging.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Blind restoration trains one network over wide severity ranges without telling it the severity, expecting implicit estimation to emerge.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Networks trained blind over mixed severities partially average incompatible inverse operators rather than cleanly inferring severity per input, so an identical network given a coarse severity signal (even a noisy estimate) outperforms the blind version across the entire severity range at matched capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Severity-conditioned models will beat blind models uniformly across the severity axis, and the blind model's per-severity behavior will match a mixture-weighted average of specialists rather than the best specialist per severity.
why_important: If a one-scalar conditioning input yields uniform gains, the standard blind formulation wastes quality for an unnecessary purity constraint.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Conditioning on degradation parameters exists; characterizing blind training as measurable operator-averaging with a specialist-mixture signature may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train specialists per severity band, a blind model, and a conditioned model at matched capacity; compare per-severity curves and test whether blind behavior matches the specialist mixture prediction.
main_risk: With enough capacity the blind model may internally route severities well, making the effect capacity-dependent.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Blind models are assumed to learn internal severity estimation that approaches conditioned performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Severity inference from small receptive fields is uncertain, and under uncertainty the loss-minimizing response is operator averaging; averaging incompatible inverses produces outputs no single severity would want.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one public blind model against the same architecture fine-tuned with an oracle severity input on a severity sweep; a uniform conditioned advantage on the sweep makes the case quickly.

one_line_idea: Overparameterized SR models memorize training patches retrievably: nearest-neighbor probes on outputs would reveal patch-level copying, qualifying texture-generalization claims.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Modern SR models have capacity far exceeding classical estimates of task complexity and train for many epochs over finite patch distributions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable fraction of synthesized high-frequency content in SR outputs consists of near-copies of specific training patches (retrievable by patch-level nearest-neighbor search), concentrated in stochastic texture regions, so texture synthesis is partly patch recall rather than distributional generalization.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Patch-retrieval probes against the training set will find above-chance near-duplicate matches for output texture patches, at rates increasing with model capacity and training epochs and decreasing with training-set size.
why_important: Patch recall affects both intellectual-property questions and scientific claims about what SR models learned; it also predicts brittleness on genuinely novel textures.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Memorization probes exist for generative models at the image level; patch-level memorization audits for SR texture synthesis may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Index the training patch corpus, run retrieval on output texture patches versus matched controls (real photos, other models), and quantify near-duplication rates across capacity and data scales.
main_risk: Generic texture similarity produces retrieval hits without memorization, so control baselines and similarity thresholds carry the burden of proof.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] SR texture synthesis is assumed to reflect learned texture statistics rather than recallable instances.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reconstruction training explicitly rewards reproducing training targets; with excess capacity and repeated exposure, storing high-value patches is the loss-optimal use of parameters.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one small SR model trained on a modest known corpus, retrieve nearest training patches for its synthesized textures on a few outputs; conspicuous near-duplicates in the first probes demonstrate patch recall.

one_line_idea: Iterative refinement helps sampling, not restoration: at matched compute, single-pass fidelity models match multi-step ones, and iteration only pays when the goal is drawing from a distribution.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multi-step inference (diffusion, iterative refinement) dominates recent restoration research, spending several forward passes per image, while single-pass regressors remain far cheaper.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For evidence-bounded fidelity objectives, iteration adds nothing fundamental: a single-pass model with the iteration compute folded into its capacity matches multi-step fidelity, and iteration's real value is exclusively in distributional sampling for perceptual texture.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Iso-compute comparisons will show single-pass models matching multi-step ones on fidelity metrics across degradations, with multi-step advantages confined to realism metrics and sample diversity.
why_important: It separates what iteration buys from what scale buys, guiding deployment (fidelity products can skip iteration entirely) and clarifying why distillation works when it works.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Speed-quality comparisons exist per paper; a clean iso-compute fidelity-versus-sampling decomposition of iteration's value in restoration may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train single-pass models sized to match multi-step inference FLOPs, compare fidelity and realism metric families separately across degradation types and severities.
main_risk: Training dynamics may prevent single-pass models from using the extra capacity effectively, confounding representational and optimization explanations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Iterative refinement is assumed intrinsically superior for restoration quality, justifying its inference cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fidelity-optimal restoration is a deterministic function of the input (the posterior mean or similar); deterministic functions have no intrinsic need for iterative stochastic computation, only distribution sampling does.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare a strong public single-pass model against a diffusion restorer constrained to equal wall-clock compute on fidelity metrics; parity on the sample would already challenge the iteration narrative.

one_line_idea: Test-time geometric self-ensembling gains expose a fixable equivariance defect: equivariance-regularized training recovers the ensemble's benefit in a single pass.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Averaging predictions over flips and rotations at test time reliably improves SR metrics, a practice used for years at multiplied inference cost.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The self-ensemble gain measures the model's violation of geometric equivariance, and adding an equivariance-consistency loss during training removes most of the violation, delivering self-ensemble-level quality in one forward pass and eliminating the standard justification for eightfold inference.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The single-pass performance of equivariance-trained models will approach their own self-ensembled performance, and the residual self-ensemble gain will shrink toward zero as the consistency weight increases, without harming baseline quality.
why_important: It converts a costly inference heuristic into a free training-time property, and establishes the ensemble gain as a useful diagnostic of learned-operator symmetry defects.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Equivariant architectures exist; interpreting self-ensemble gains as trainable violation energy and closing them with a consistency loss in SR may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with increasing equivariance-consistency weights, measure single-pass quality and residual self-ensemble gain per weight, and verify the gain shrinks as violation shrinks.
main_risk: True scene statistics are not perfectly symmetric (gravity, lighting priors), so full equivariance could slightly hurt oriented-content restoration.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Self-ensembling is treated as a free-lunch inference trick rather than as evidence of a training deficiency.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A gain from averaging over transformed inputs exists only if the model disagrees with its own transformed predictions; the disagreement is a measurable, penalizable training residual, not an inherent limit.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Measure per-image correlation between self-ensemble gain and an equivariance-violation score for one public model; a strong correlation confirms the mechanism and motivates the training fix.
